    Engine · the feedback loops

    Learning Loops

    The five ways the room learns — journal lessons fed back into prompts, per-member dossiers, an outcome model the Executive reads, the RL population's nightly generation, and the Fund's allocation transformer — and, just as exactly, what none of them learns yet.

    Five loops, one day#

    Bablytics learns in five places, and they close at different speeds. Two are in words and three are in numbers. All five are fed by the same two facts the day produces: the grades the board wrote in the morning, and what the tape did afterwards — the 16:45 realized outcomes and the close the Evening Court scores against.

    The first four are drawn below. The fifth — the Fund's allocation transformer, added in round 27 — hangs off the same court night and is described in its own section; its diagram is the Fund's daily cycle, because what it learns is a portfolio decision, not a grade.

    Loop 1 — lessons into prompts#

    At the Evening Court every member — the thirteen graders, the Skeptic and the Executive — files a self-review against their own morning grades and the realized day returns: where they were on base, where they were off base, and the durable lesson they take. The entries are persisted to member_journal. The next morning, in real (API-key) mode, every seat's prompt — each grader's, the Skeptic's and the Executive's — is prefixed with that seat's five most recent lessons under the heading "YOUR TRADING JOURNAL — lessons from your recent sessions (apply them)". The loop is a paragraph of text, which is exactly why it is the most legible of the four: you can read what a seat learned on its Boardroom card, its member page, and its dossier, and you can see it re-used the next day.

    Two smaller word-loops ride alongside. The Pyramid re-forms every evening on realized returns (stance × conviction × underlying move, EWMA over ten sessions), and every morning prompt carries the member's rank one-liner while the Executive's carries the full standings and is told to weight the leader's grades more (in mock mode, literally 1.5×). And the owner's reflections on taken trades are handed to the Executive's court prompt verbatim. Mock mode is honest about this loop's limits: the deterministic board does not read prompts, so in mock mode the journals are filed but not applied.

    Loop 2 — dossiers#

    After the journals are persisted the court regenerates one markdown file per seat under data/members/<key>.md (plus an index): the journal newest-first, the grading history — up to sixty graded leads with the member's grade, stance, the board's final grade, the realized 5-day return and the comment — the pyramid standing, and calibration (graded leads with outcomes and the grade-to-return correlation). The same data backs /api/member/{key}/dossier. Nothing in the app re-reads the files into a prompt; they exist so a person, or an agent convening a court by hand, has a single readable record of what each seat has been saying and how it turned out. They are the learning loop's paper trail, not a gradient.

    Loop 3 — the outcome model the Executive reads#

    The oldest loop is numeric. A small sklearn network — MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(32, 16)) in a pipeline behind a StandardScaler — learns to predict a lead's 5-day realized return from a 24-number vector: the thirteen members' grades in roster order (a missing grade is 50, a neutral read) followed by eleven numeric features from the scan and the technicals (options score, volume ratio, volume-to-OI, call/put ratio, 1-day and 5-day change, RSI-14, distance to support and resistance, above the 50- and 200-day). It trains once at least 25 rows have a 5-day outcome; with 40 or more it reports 80/20 hold-out MAE and R² and then refits on everything, and below that it says plainly that the metrics are in-sample. It is retrained at 16:45 after outcomes are recorded and again at the top of every morning run.

    Its output reaches the room in two ways. The pipeline calls predict_many on each morning's candidates before the board has graded, so the grade slots are all 50 and the prediction rides on the numeric features alone; the Executive's prompt then carries the predicted return per candidate and per-member calibration — sample size, hit rate, grade-to-return correlation — so consistently wrong seats are discounted and consistently right ones weighted up. Calibration is also shown on the Boardroom and member pages.

    Its numbers, as of this writing. The sidecar at data/model.json records a model trained on 60 rows with hold-out MAE 5.29 percentage points and R² 0.05. That is a model that explains almost none of the variance in 5-day returns — which is the honest state of a 24-feature regression after a few weeks of twenty leads a day. The Executive is told it is a read, not a ruling.

    Loop 4 — the RL population#

    The fourth loop is the Pulse's five actor-critic models, and it is the only one that breeds: it retires and replaces members rather than just refitting one. The court's last act, after journals and dossiers, is one generation: score every member, train every member on the day's fresh episodes, breed one mutated child from the elite, and admit the child only if its fitness on a frozen held-out split beats the worst member's — the elite is never replaced, the population never shrinks, and a generation that changes nothing is recorded with the same fields as one that does. The first generation (2026-08-21) refused its child and left m1–m5 standing. The full mechanism — the fitness formula, the held-out split, the rejection record, the model card's caveats — is on the Pulse page.

    Loop 5 — the Fund's allocation transformer#

    The fifth loop learns a different kind of thing. Loops ③ and ④ learn about a position — what a lead will return, what to do about one you hold. The Fund's transformer learns about the book as a whole: given the last twenty sessions of book statistics, realized feedback and regime, what fraction a ∈ [0, 1] of the portfolio belongs in the board's ≥60 book today, and how should that fraction be split across the open lots. It is hand-written numpy — embedding, two causal self-attention blocks, an allocation head and a shared per-lot scoring head — and it imports the same Adam the Pulse's population uses. The full mechanism is on The Fund.

    Like loop ④ it trains inside the Evening Court (fund.train.nightly(), gated by fund_train_enabled, with a deeper weekly pass on Sunday), and like loop ④ it deploys only through a gate: a candidate checkpoint must beat the incumbent on a frozen held-out slice — the last 20 % of sessions by date — on both the allocation loss and the weight ranking, and be no more than 10 % worse on any risk profile. Deployments and rejections alike, with their numbers, land in data/fund/meta.json and data/fund/self-court.jsonl, and the Fund's Model card shows the recent decisions as dated chips. A stale feature hash raises instead of loading, the same rule as the Pulse's.

    Two honesty devices this loop needs and the others do not. First, shrinkage: while the effective training days sit below fund_min_train_days (default 60), the deployed allocation is pulled halfway toward a prior derived from your stated risk and size goals, and the payload says "shrunk": true and why. Second, the simulacrum label: the board has only ever produced on the order of fifteen live runs, so training is extended backwards with reconstructed pseudo-runs built from numeric features alone — momentum, ATR, RSI, volume ratio, sector. Those days are not the board and are labelled as such in the checkpoint. Half of what the dial shows you, at this sample size, is your own goal setting.

    What is learned — and what is not#

    Learned#

    • Each seat's last five lessons, as text in its prompt (real mode).
    • Each seat's pyramid rank and the leader's extra weight.
    • Per-member calibration: sample size, hit rate, grade→return correlation.
    • The outcome MLP's weights, retrained twice a day.
    • The five RL members' weights, their fitness, and the roster's lineage.
    • The fitness-weighted consensus weights the Pulse votes with.
    • The Fund's allocation transformer: how much of the portfolio belongs in the ≥60 book, and the relative weight of each lot in it.

    Not learned — fixed by code#

    • Exit zones: ATR multiples per profile, arithmetic.
    • The blend overrides: grade ≤ 40, VIX 16 / SPY 770, agreement ≤ 0.6.
    • The Bailiff's parser, bases and clock.
    • The League's 10 % sizing and five-day hold.
    • The grading rubric and each persona's system prompt.
    • The pyramid's scoring formula and its ten-session span.
    • Inside the RL state: the written-kill distance, session progress and board grade — silenced because training has never seen them vary.
    • The Fund's admission bar (60), its position cap (20), its exit rules and horizon slack, and every tax rate and threshold in its tax lens — all settings and arithmetic.

    Honest limits#

    • Loop 1 only closes in real mode. Mock personas are rules; a lesson can be filed but cannot change a rule. In mock mode the journals are a record, not a feedback.
    • Loop 3 has sixty rows. R² 0.05 on hold-out is not a forecast. The predicted-return column in the Executive's prompt is labelled as model output and the Executive's own track record — the final grades' correlation to realized return — is what the court grades.
    • Loop 4's objective is shaped reward, not money. Every member's fitness is negative; "beats buy-and-hold" means "cuts exposure"; the ensemble does not beat its best single member; the most predictive column the system has found is one the networks have never been trained on. The model card says all of this in full and this site does not soften it.
    • Loop 5 has the smallest real sample of all of them. A transformer on a few dozen genuine sessions is a transformer on nothing; the honest parts of it are the shrinkage toward your stated goals, the label on the reconstructed history, and the gate that rejects most candidates. Read its dial as a temperament, not a forecast.
    • None of the loops touches the rules that decide what happens to a position — zones, overrides, kills, sizing. Those are read off the page; that is a design choice, so that what is learned is always the opinion and never the safety rail.
    • Nothing learned anywhere can reach an order. The Pulse and the Bailiff have no execution path; the only code that submits a real order is the one-order-per-click Broker flow, and no loop calls it.

    Where to see each loop#

    Boardroom → member cards
    the JOURNAL strip (latest lesson, entry count) and calibration
    #/member/<key>
    overview, grading history with realized returns, analysis archive, journal, paper book
    Dashboard → Evening view · the Evening Court PDF
    the court's scoreboard and every seat's ON BASE / OFF BASE / LESSON; the MODELS AND TRAINING appendix with the night's generation lives in the live-board court document (data/boardroom/<date>/) and in data/boardroom/<date>/generation.json, not in the in-app PDF
    Pulse → Model card
    the population panel, the last self-court verdict, the decision strip
    Fund → Model card
    the checkpoint, the honestly-labelled training data, the held-out numbers and the last gate decisions — deployed and rejected alike (the gate)
    Archive · Reviews
    run history with 1-day and 5-day columns; the week review's per-member accuracy
    data/members/ · data/rl/self-court.jsonl · data/model.json · data/fund/self-court.jsonl
    the dossiers, the generation ledger, the outcome model's metrics, the Fund's gate history
